modal-dialog.summary: A dialog that pauses the current task for a decision.
modal-dialog.description: A modal dialog asks for a decision or a short input. While it's open, the rest of the page is unavailable.

drawer.summary: A panel that slides in from the edge of the screen.
drawer.description: A drawer opens a panel from the edge of the screen for filters, details, or longer input while the current screen stays in place.

popover.summary: A small panel with more information or actions next to a control.
popover.description: A popover opens a small panel near its trigger with extra explanation, links, or simple controls, without leaving the current context. Unlike a modal, the page behind it stays usable.

tooltip.summary: A short hint shown on hover or keyboard focus.
tooltip.description: A tooltip shows a short supporting explanation when people hover over or focus an icon or term. Its content must be plain text that can't be clicked.

bottom-sheet.summary: A task panel that slides up from the bottom of the screen.
bottom-sheet.description: A bottom sheet raises a panel from the bottom edge with a few choices or next actions. The options sit within thumb reach, so people can pick quickly on mobile and return to the screen they were on.

dropdown-menu.summary: A list of actions that opens from a button.
dropdown-menu.description: A dropdown menu lists related actions right below a button. Actions people use less often are kept in one place and come out only when needed, which keeps the screen tidy.

alert-dialog.summary: An urgent message that needs a response.
alert-dialog.description: An alert dialog reports something people must know and answer now, such as an expiring session or a failed payment. The system usually opens it, not a click, and clicking the backdrop does not close it.

context-menu.summary: A menu opened by right-clicking or long-pressing an item.
context-menu.description: A context menu appears where people right-click or long-press an object such as a file or message, listing what they can do with it. It's a fast shortcut for people who know it's there.

command-palette.summary: A command box opened with ⌘K to search and run actions.
command-palette.description: A command palette opens with a keyboard shortcut; people type what they want to do and run the matching command right away. Features buried deep in menus are a few keystrokes away, which speeds up experienced users.

hover-card.summary: A preview card that appears when hovering a link.
hover-card.description: A hover card shows a summary of a person or link when the pointer rests on it for a moment, so people can see who or what it is without leaving the page.

confirmation-dialog.summary: A dialog that asks once more before continuing.
confirmation-dialog.description: A confirmation dialog asks whether to continue or cancel right before something hard to undo. Wrapped in a Promise, it reads as one line, await confirm(), so each screen doesn't have to manage its own modal state.

toast.summary: A short result message that appears and then disappears.
toast.description: A toast briefly shows the result of an action at the top or bottom of the screen and disappears on its own. It confirms the result without interrupting the task, and can carry a short action such as undo (a snackbar).

alert-banner.summary: A message at the top of the page that stays until dismissed.
alert-banner.description: An alert banner stays at the top of a page or section until people read it or act on it. Its tone follows the severity: information, success, warning, or error.

inline-validation.summary: A message right below a field that says what's wrong.
inline-validation.description: Inline validation shows why an input is wrong and how to fix it right below that field, so people know at once where to make the change.

error-summary.summary: A list of errors above the form, with links to each field.
error-summary.description: An error summary gathers everything to fix above a form that failed to submit. People see how many things went wrong, and each item jumps to its field.

undo.summary: A snackbar that reverses an action such as delete.
undo.description: Undo applies an easy-to-regret action such as delete on screen first and gives a short window to take it back; only then is it final. It interrupts the flow less than asking for confirmation every time.

callout.summary: A note or warning box inside body text.
callout.description: A callout sets apart something worth noticing in help or documentation with a colored box and a title. Kinds such as note, tip, and warning tell readers how important it is.

notification-center.summary: A panel that collects past notifications.
notification-center.description: A notification center shows the unread count on a bell icon and opens a panel of recent notifications when pressed, so people can catch up on toasts they missed.

progress-toast.summary: A progress notice for a long-running task.
progress-toast.description: A progress toast shows a long task such as an upload or export in a corner of the screen. People can follow the progress, keep working, and cancel if needed.

confirmation-message.summary: What happens next, shown after a form is sent.
confirmation-message.description: A confirmation message replaces a sent form with the result and the next steps: what was received, when and how people will hear back, and what they can do now.

push-notification.summary: A system notification that reaches people outside the app.
push-notification.description: Push notifications use the browser or operating system to deliver news when people aren't looking at the app. Show what they will receive first, and ask for permission only when they want it.

breadcrumb.summary: A row of links showing where the page sits in the site.
breadcrumb.description: A breadcrumb shows the parent path to the current page on one line, so people can tell where they are and jump up a level in one step.

pagination.summary: Numbered buttons that split a long list into pages.
pagination.description: Pagination splits many results into pages of a fixed size, moved through with page numbers and previous and next buttons. People can remember a position and find it again.

navbar.summary: The menu for the whole site.
navbar.description: A navbar is the site menu in the same place at the top of every page: a logo, a few main links, and a key action on the right. It marks the page people are on.

sidebar-navigation.summary: A menu fixed to the left side.
sidebar-navigation.description: Sidebar navigation keeps a vertical menu fixed on the left. Many items stay visible at once, and related items fold into groups. It's common in admin tools and work apps.

bottom-tab-bar.summary: Switching between the main screens on mobile.
bottom-tab-bar.description: A bottom tab bar lines up three to five main screens with icons and names at the bottom of a mobile screen. It sits within thumb reach, so people can move between screens with one hand.

stepper.summary: Shows the current step and finished steps in a multi-step flow.
stepper.description: A stepper shows all the steps of an ordered flow such as sign-up or checkout, where people are, and what they've finished. Knowing how many steps are left makes it easier to see it through.

mobile-menu.summary: A menu folded away on small screens.
mobile-menu.description: A mobile menu folds the site menu into one button on small screens and opens it when pressed. The screen stays roomy while every menu item stays reachable.

infinite-scroll.summary: Loading more when the end is reached.
infinite-scroll.description: Infinite scroll loads and appends the next batch automatically as people near the end of a list. In feeds made for browsing, it removes the work of turning pages.

load-more.description: Load more appends the next batch only when people press the button at the end of the list. It shows how many items they've seen out of the total, and moves focus to the first new item so reading continues.

mega-menu.summary: A menu that opens into several columns.
mega-menu.description: A mega menu opens a wide panel of sub-links in several columns from a top menu item. For sites with many pages, such as products and solutions, it shows the structure at once.

table-of-contents.summary: A table of contents that follows the scroll position.
table-of-contents.description: A table of contents lists the sections of a long document alongside it and marks the one being read, so people can check where they are and jump to any section.

back-to-top.summary: A way back to the start of a long page.
back-to-top.description: A back-to-top button appears only after people scroll well down a long page and takes them back to the top. It then moves focus to the top heading so keyboard users continue from the start.

back-navigation.summary: Going back to where you were, with the list's scroll restored.
back-navigation.description: Back navigation restores the scroll position and opened item when people return from a detail screen to a list, so they continue instead of searching again from the top.

horizontal-scroll.description: Horizontal scroll lays several cards in a row that people browse sideways: swiped by hand, or moved one screen at a time with previous and next buttons on wide screens.

tabs.summary: A menu that switches between related content on the same screen.
tabs.description: Tabs split related content into panels and show one panel at a time, so people can switch quickly between information at the same level without leaving the page.

accordion.summary: A vertical list whose titles open and close their content.
accordion.description: An accordion shows only the titles of several sections at first, and people press the ones they want to open. It fits long information into a short screen.

read-more.description: Read more shows a few lines of a long description and expands the full text in place when people press it. Lists and cards stay short, and anyone who wants to can read to the end.

disclosure.summary: Opening and closing a single block.
disclosure.description: A disclosure is the simplest way to open and close content: press one title to show or hide what's under it. Folding away information people rarely need keeps the screen light.

tree-view.description: A tree view shows folders within folders as an indented list, and people open only the branches they need. It handles deep data such as file explorers and org charts.

collapsible-panel.summary: A side area that folds to the side.
collapsible-panel.description: A collapsible panel folds a side area such as properties, filters, or comments into a narrow bar so the main content gets more room. A button on the bar opens it again any time.

scrollable-tabs.summary: Scrolling tabs sideways when they overflow.
scrollable-tabs.description: Scrollable tabs let people scroll sideways when there are too many tabs for one row. Arrows at both ends scroll them, and the selected tab always moves into view.

text-field.summary: A basic input with a label, a hint, an error, and a required mark.
text-field.description: A text field takes a single line of text. It bundles an always-visible label, a format hint, an error message for wrong input, and whether it's required, so every form uses it the same way.

password-field.summary: Show and hide, with rule checks.
password-field.description: A password field hides what's typed but lets people check it with an eye icon, and ticks off each rule as they type. People find problems before they submit, not after.

search-field.summary: A search input with a clear button and a shortcut.
search-field.description: A search field adds a clear button and a jump-to shortcut (/) to the search input. The list narrows as people type, and the query can be cleared and retyped in one step.

otp-input.summary: A code input split into boxes.
otp-input.description: An OTP input takes a short numeric code from a text message or email, one digit per box. Typing moves to the next box, and pasting or SMS autofill fills them all at once.

textarea.summary: Grows with its content and shows a character count.
textarea.description: A textarea takes several lines of text, grows to fit what's written, and shows how many characters are left. People can see and edit the whole text without it being trapped in a scroll box.

number-stepper.summary: Adjusting a quantity with − and + buttons.
number-stepper.description: A number stepper changes a small whole number such as a quantity one step at a time with − and + buttons, and accepts typing in the middle box. At the minimum or maximum, the button turns off and says why.

input-mask.summary: Automatic dashes for phone and card numbers.
input-mask.description: An input mask adds dashes or spaces in the right places while people type only digits. They don't have to think about the format, and the stored value keeps only the digits, which is easier for the server.

tag-input.summary: A field where typed words stack up as chips.
tag-input.description: A tag input turns a word into a chip when people press Enter or a comma. Several keywords go into one field, and each chip can be removed on its own.

multi-step-form.summary: Splitting a long form into steps.
multi-step-form.description: A multi-step form splits a long form into steps by topic, with a progress indicator and previous and next buttons. People see less at once, and they review their answers before submitting at the end.

floating-label.summary: A label that moves up once you type.
floating-label.description: A floating label sits inside the field and moves up, smaller, when the field gets focus or a value. It saves vertical space, and the label stays visible after input.

switch.summary: A setting that turns on or off as soon as it's pressed.
switch.description: A switch shows two states, on and off, and applies the change the moment it's pressed. Like a light switch, there's no save button.

segmented-control.summary: Joined buttons for choosing one of two to five options.
segmented-control.description: A segmented control lines up a few mutually exclusive options as joined buttons and lets people pick one. It's often used to view the same data by a different measure or layout.

checkbox.summary: Choosing items independently, including a partly selected state.
checkbox.description: Checked values are used when submitting a form or acting on several items at once. When only some items are picked, the select-all checkbox shows an in-between state.

radio-group.description: A radio group lays out all the options and lets people choose exactly one. Because the options can be compared at a glance, it works well for choices that differ in price or terms.

select.summary: A dropdown for choosing one item from a list.
select.description: A select is a dropdown for choosing one item from a fixed list. Styling the native select element keeps the operating system's picker on phones and its keyboard and assistive technology support.

combobox.summary: Autocomplete that narrows choices as you type.
combobox.description: A combobox keeps only the options that match what people type and lets them pick one. A long list can be searched with a few letters instead of scrolling.

filter-chip.summary: Filters you press to turn on and off.
filter-chip.description: Filter chips line up short conditions above a list and turn them on and off when pressed. Results update right away, so people can add and remove conditions one at a time until they find what they want.

multi-select.summary: Picking several items and showing them as chips.
multi-select.description: A multi-select opens a list from a button where people check several items, and shows the chosen ones as chips. It takes several values without taking much room.

slider.description: A slider picks a value in a range by dragging a handle along a bar. It works well for quickly trying rough values and watching the result, rather than entering an exact number.

range-slider.summary: Choosing a minimum and a maximum together.
range-slider.description: A range slider sets a minimum and a maximum with two handles on one bar. It's for filters by range, such as a price band or a period.

listbox.summary: Choosing from a list that stays open.
listbox.description: A listbox keeps its options open and lets people choose one. Each option can carry a description, and people move up and down with the keyboard to choose right away.

date-picker.summary: Choosing a day on a calendar.
date-picker.description: A date picker opens a calendar from a button and lets people choose a day while seeing the whole month. Weekdays and weeks are visible together, which makes nearby dates easy to pick.

file-upload.summary: An area for dragging and dropping files.
file-upload.description: A file upload takes files dropped in or chosen with a button. It states the allowed types and sizes up front, rejects files that don't fit with the reason, and lets people remove uploaded files from the list.

date-range-picker.summary: Choosing a start date and an end date.
date-range-picker.description: A date range picker selects a period by pressing a start date and then an end date on the calendar. Like a hotel check-in and check-out, it shows both dates and the days between.

time-picker.description: A time picker sets a time by choosing the hour and the minute separately. Showing only the allowed range, such as opening hours, and fixed steps, such as every 10 minutes, keeps wrong times out.

calendar.description: A calendar shows a month with dots on days that have events, and lists a day's events when it's pressed. People see the shape of the month and the details of a day together.

image-cropper.description: An image cropper lets people drag a photo and zoom it with a slider to choose what fits in a round frame. A small preview shows how it will actually look.

color-picker.summary: Choosing a color from a palette or a spectrum.
color-picker.description: A color picker offers a few preset colors as round swatches, and the browser's color chooser for any other color. The chosen color shows in a preview and as a color code.

signature-pad.description: A signature pad takes a signature drawn with a finger or mouse inside a box and keeps it as an image. People can clear and redraw it, and those who find drawing hard can type their name instead.

date-input.summary: Typing a date in a set format and checking it.
date-input.description: A date input adds the dots as people type only digits in YYYY.MM.DD format, and checks that the date exists once it's complete. For distant dates such as a birthday, it's much faster than paging through a calendar.

quick-date-chips.summary: Choosing common dates such as today, tomorrow, or this weekend in one tap.
quick-date-chips.description: Quick date chips show the dates people choose most, such as today, tomorrow, and this weekend, as chips they can pick in one tap. Any other date can be chosen right below.

time-slots.summary: Choosing one of the times open for booking.
time-slots.description: Time slots show bookable times as a grid of buttons and mark the taken ones as full. Once a time is chosen, the booking button names it, which prevents mistakes.

month-picker.summary: Choosing only a year and a month, without a day.
month-picker.description: A month picker lets people page through years and press one of twelve months to choose a year and month only. It's for places that don't need a day, such as billing, statements, and monthly reports.

wheel-picker.summary: Rolling a vertical wheel to choose a date or time.
wheel-picker.description: A wheel picker lets people flick vertical columns with a finger and choose the value in the middle row. It's familiar on mobile screens that set several columns together, such as an alarm time.

recurrence-picker.summary: Setting how often, on which days, and until when something repeats.
recurrence-picker.description: A recurrence picker splits how often, on which weekdays, and until when an event repeats into separate choices, and states the resulting rule as one sentence so even complex rules can be read and checked.

button.summary: The hierarchy and states of primary, secondary, and text buttons.
button.description: Buttons with three levels of emphasis put the actions on a screen in order. Only the most important action gets the primary button, and each button looks different on hover, on press, and on keyboard focus.

icon-button.summary: A button with an icon and no text.
icon-button.description: An icon button is a small button that shows its action with an icon instead of words. Its name is given to assistive technology, and the same name appears as a tooltip on hover or keyboard focus.

loading-button.summary: Shows work in progress after a press, then success or failure.
loading-button.description: A loading button shows that work is in progress right where it was pressed, then changes to success or failure when it's done. People see the result in the button, and it can't be pressed twice while working.

disabled-button.summary: A button that says why it can't be pressed.
disabled-button.description: A disabled button doesn't just look faded: it says right below why it can't be pressed yet. Pressing it anyway highlights the reason so people know what to do.

toggle-button.summary: Keeps its on or off state after it's pressed.
toggle-button.description: A toggle button turns on when pressed and off when pressed again. It's used in formatting tools such as bold and italic, where several can be on together, and its on state stays visible.

fab.summary: The main action, floating above the screen.
fab.description: A floating action button stays in a corner of the screen while people scroll. Scrolling down shrinks it to an icon so it covers less content, and scrolling up shows its name again.

copy-button.summary: Press to copy, then see the result.
copy-button.description: A copy button puts a link or code on the clipboard and briefly changes to "Copied" in place to confirm it. If copying is blocked, it says so too.

split-button.summary: A default action together with other options.
split-button.description: A split button runs the common action in one press and offers similar actions behind the arrow beside it. It's for a family of actions, such as save and save as.

hold-to-confirm.summary: Press and hold to prevent mistakes.
hold-to-confirm.description: Hold to confirm runs an action that can't be undone, such as delete, only after the button is held for a moment. The button fills while held, and letting go early cancels it.

list.summary: Rows with an icon, a title, and extra details.
list.description: A list gathers an icon, a title, a second line, and a value on the right into one row so people can scan many items. The whole row is one button, so pressing anywhere opens it.

data-table.summary: Comparing and sorting data by column.
data-table.description: A data table compares values in rows and columns and sorts them when a column header is pressed. Numbers align right with fixed-width digits, and the header stays in place on scroll.

selectable-table.summary: Choosing several rows and acting on them at once.
selectable-table.description: A selectable table puts a checkbox on each row so people can choose several and archive or delete them at once. Once rows are chosen, the count and the action buttons appear above.

description-list.description: A description list lays out information that comes in label and value pairs, such as an order number or payment method. Wide screens show two columns; narrow screens put the value under its label.

timeline.description: A timeline lines up events in time order along a vertical line. It shows what happened, where things stand now, and the steps still ahead in one column.

kanban-board.description: A kanban board places tasks as cards in columns by status and moves them to the next status by dragging. For people who can't drag, each card also has buttons to move it to the previous or next column.

sortable-list.description: A sortable list changes the order of items by dragging a handle. With a keyboard, people focus the handle and move it with the up and down arrows, and the new position is announced.

grouped-list.summary: A grouped list whose headers stick as you scroll.
grouped-list.description: A grouped list splits a long list by initial letter or date and keeps the current group's header stuck at the top while scrolling, so people always know where they are.

virtualized-list.description: A virtualized list draws only the few rows visible on screen out of thousands, so even very long lists stay fast. The full height is kept, so the scrollbar shows the real position.

card.summary: One tile with an image, a title, and a summary.
card.description: A card bundles an image, a title, and a short summary into one box so many pieces of content can sit side by side. Pressing anywhere opens it, but the only link is the title, which keeps screen readers concise.

carousel.summary: A set of cards that slide sideways.
carousel.description: A carousel shows banners or photos one at a time and moves through them with previous and next buttons and dots. When it advances on its own, it pauses on hover or focus and has a pause button.

image-gallery.description: An image gallery lines up small thumbnails under a large photo, and pressing a thumbnail swaps the large one. It's for looking at a product from several angles in turn.

lightbox.summary: Showing an image large and paging through.
lightbox.description: A lightbox opens a small photo large over the screen and lets people page through left and right. It shows the photo's position, such as 2 of 4, with its caption, and closing it returns to the photo that was pressed.

masonry-grid.summary: Cards of different heights stacked like bricks.
masonry-grid.description: A masonry grid stacks cards of different heights without gaps, like a brick wall. Photos with different proportions aren't cropped, and the number of columns follows the screen width.

before-after-slider.summary: Dragging the middle to compare two images.
before-after-slider.description: A before/after slider layers two images of the same scene and shows more of one as people drag the handle in the middle. It shows the difference before and after editing or renovation at a glance.

stories.description: Stories show short pieces of content full screen, one at a time, moving on after a while or when people tap the side. Bars at the top show the current story's position among the rest.

badge.description: A badge puts a small number on an icon to show new notifications or items in a cart. Large numbers shorten to "99+", and the badge disappears when there's nothing to count.

status-dot.summary: Success, warning, and error as colored dots.
status-dot.description: A status dot shows the state of a service or task with a green, yellow, or red dot and a short word. It never relies on color alone; the word is always there.

tag.summary: A small label for a category.
tag.description: A tag attaches the category or topic of a post or item as a small label. In edit views, each tag can have a remove button.

avatar.summary: A photo or initials that stand for a person.
avatar.description: An avatar shows a person as a photo in a small circle, and falls back to the first letter of their name when there's no photo or it fails to load. The same person always gets the same color.

avatar-group.description: An avatar group overlaps several people's avatars and shortens the rest to a number such as "+3". It shows who's involved even in a tight space.

page-indicator.summary: Dots showing the current slide of a carousel.
page-indicator.description: A page indicator uses dots to show which of a few screens people are on. The current dot differs in length as well as color.

unread-indicator.description: An unread indicator puts a blue dot before items in a list that haven't been opened and sets their titles in bold. Opening an item removes both.

presence.description: Presence puts a small dot on the corner of an avatar to show whether the person is online or away. People can change their own status.

feature-dot.summary: A dot on a newly added menu item.
feature-dot.description: A feature dot draws attention to a new menu item and disappears once it's opened. A dot that stays after it's been seen means nothing, so whether it was opened is remembered.

scroll-progress.summary: A bar at the top showing how far you've read.
scroll-progress.description: Scroll progress fills a thin bar at the very top as people read a long article, so they can tell at a glance how much is left.

password-strength-meter.summary: Shows the strength of a password with levels and words.
password-strength-meter.description: A password strength meter shows strength with a four-part bar and words such as weak, fair, and strong while people type, plus one line on how to make it stronger.

sticky-header.summary: A top bar that stays while you scroll.
sticky-header.description: A sticky header keeps the title and main actions at the top of the screen as people scroll down a list. A shadow appears only once content starts passing underneath, so it looks light the rest of the time.

sticky-action-bar.summary: A main button that's always visible on mobile.
sticky-action-bar.description: A sticky action bar keeps the price and the buy button at the bottom of the screen while people read the product details. It sits within thumb reach, so they can act right away.

split-view.summary: A list and its details side by side.
split-view.description: A split view puts a list and its details side by side on wide screens and shows one at a time on narrow ones. It responds to the width of its own area (a container query), not the window.

sidebar-layout.summary: Two columns: a menu and the content.
sidebar-layout.description: A sidebar layout puts the menu on the left and the content on the right. When space runs short, the menu moves to a row above the content.

responsive-grid.summary: A grid whose column count changes with the width.
responsive-grid.description: A responsive grid only sets the minimum width of a cell and creates as many columns as fit. Without breakpoints, cells fill evenly at any width.

bento-grid.summary: Fitting cells of different sizes together.
bento-grid.description: A bento grid fills tiles of different sizes without gaps, like a lunch box, to introduce features. The largest tile carries the main point and the smaller ones support it.

safe-area.summary: Padding that avoids the notch and home bar.
safe-area.description: Safe area padding adds env(safe-area-inset-*) so a phone's notch, rounded corners, and home indicator never cover content.

hero-section.summary: The key headline and main action in the first area of the page.
hero-section.description: A hero section uses the first area visitors see to say what the service does: a one-line headline, a one-sentence description, and a single main button.

card-grid.summary: Repeating cards in an even grid.
card-grid.description: A card grid places cards of the same shape in an even grid and aligns each card's content vertically so the button rows line up even when titles differ in length.

dashboard-layout.summary: Metric cards and charts in reading order.
dashboard-layout.description: A dashboard layout puts the most important numbers in cards at the top, a chart of their trend in the middle, and a detailed table at the bottom. Changing the period updates everything together.

magazine-layout.summary: Lead and supporting content told apart by size and position.
magazine-layout.description: A magazine layout shows one lead story large and stacks the rest small beside it, using size and position to show importance. On narrow screens, everything stacks in one column starting with the lead.

z-pattern.summary: Placing information so the eye moves side to side on a simple screen.
z-pattern.description: A Z-pattern places elements along the Z-shaped path the eye follows on a sparse screen: top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right. The main action goes at the end of the path.

full-bleed.summary: Extending an image or background to the edges of the screen.
full-bleed.description: Full bleed keeps text at a comfortable reading width while letting photos and backgrounds stretch to the edges of the screen. Named grid lines do it without negative margins.

skeleton.summary: A loading state with gray shapes where the content will be.
skeleton.description: A skeleton shows gray blocks shaped like the real content while data loads. Showing the structure early makes the wait feel shorter and keeps the layout from jumping when content arrives.

spinner.summary: Waiting for a short task whose end can't be predicted.
spinner.description: A spinner shows, in a small area, that work is in progress when it's hard to tell how much is left. In the reload example, it changes to a result message when the work is done.

progress-bar.summary: Showing progress when the total amount is known.
progress-bar.description: A progress bar shows the progress of a task such as a file upload as a continuous bar. When it's done, it shows 100% together with the result.

progress-ring.description: A progress ring shows progress around the edge of a circle. On a card corner or over a thumbnail, where a bar won't fit, it still shows at a glance how far along something is.

optimistic-ui.summary: Showing the result before the response.
optimistic-ui.description: Optimistic UI assumes success and shows the result before the server responds. If the request fails, it reverts to the original state and says so briefly. Actions that rarely fail, such as a like, feel instant.

delayed-spinner.summary: A loader that doesn't appear for short waits at all.
delayed-spinner.description: A delayed spinner appears only when a wait passes a set time. Fast requests don't flash a spinner, and once one appears it stays for a minimum time so it doesn't flicker.

loading-overlay.summary: Loading that blocks a whole area.
loading-overlay.description: A loading overlay covers an area with a translucent layer while it saves and blocks input. It prevents values from changing midway and buttons from being pressed twice, and says what's in progress.

blur-up-image.summary: An image that sharpens from a blurred preview.
blur-up-image.description: A blur-up image shows a tiny blurred preview first and fades to the original when it arrives. Instead of an empty gray box, people see the photo's colors and composition early, so the wait feels shorter.

top-loading-bar.summary: A thin bar at the top that shows loading between pages.
top-loading-bar.description: A top loading bar fills a thin bar at the very top while a page or screen loads. The current screen stays in place, so nothing flickers, and quick transitions never show it at all.

pull-to-refresh.summary: Pulling the top of a list down to fetch the latest items.
pull-to-refresh.description: Pull to refresh reloads the data when people pull down and release while the scroll area is at the top. A refresh button runs the same request.

swipe-to-delete.summary: Swiping a row sideways to delete it.
swipe-to-delete.description: Swipe to delete reveals a delete button behind a row when people swipe it left, and deletes right away on a long swipe to the end. An undo appears right after, so an accidental swipe can be fixed.

drag-and-drop.summary: Dragging an item and dropping it somewhere else.
drag-and-drop.description: Drag and drop changes a card's state by dropping it in another column. Valid drop targets are highlighted during the drag, and each card has a move button that does the same, so dragging is never the only way.

long-press.summary: Pressing and holding to open a hidden menu.
long-press.description: A long press opens hidden actions such as reply and copy when an item is held for about half a second. The item shrinks slightly while held to show it's responding, and moving the finger cancels it so it isn't confused with scrolling.

swipe-to-dismiss.summary: Dragging a sheet down to close it.
swipe-to-dismiss.description: Swipe to dismiss lets a bottom sheet follow the finger down from its handle and close once it passes a set distance. Released short of that, it springs back, so it doesn't close by accident.

pinch-to-zoom.description: Pinch to zoom enlarges a map or photo when two fingers spread and shrinks it when they pinch. The zoom level is shown as text, along with zoom in, zoom out, and reset buttons that do the same.

swipe-navigation.summary: Swiping sideways to the next screen.
swipe-navigation.description: Swipe navigation moves between screens of the same kind by swiping sideways. CSS scroll snap stops exactly one screen at a time, and the current screen's title and previous and next buttons sit on top.

double-tap.summary: Double-tapping a photo to like it.
double-tap.description: A double tap on a photo likes it, with a heart that grows briefly and fades. A double tap only likes and never unlikes; the like button beside it turns the like on and off.

tap.summary: Pressing once to open or choose.
tap.description: A tap, pressing once, is the most basic gesture. Even when the visible icon is small, the touch area is at least 44×44px, and the background changes the moment it's pressed so people know it registered.

edge-swipe.summary: Swiping from the edge to open a menu.
edge-swipe.description: An edge swipe brings a menu out with the finger when people swipe right starting at the left edge of the screen. Only drags that start within 24px of the edge count, so it doesn't clash with other sideways scrolling on the page.

momentum-scrolling.summary: Scrolling that keeps going after release and slows to a stop.
momentum-scrolling.description: Momentum scrolling keeps gliding at the release speed after a fast swipe and gradually slows to a stop. Browsers already do this for touch and wheels, so the effect is added only for dragging with a mouse.

scroll-bounce.summary: Scrolling that stretches at the end and springs back.
scroll-bounce.description: Scroll bounce stretches a list by a third of the finger's distance when people pull past its start or end, and springs back on release. It lets people feel that there's no more content and keeps the page behind from scrolling.

slide-to-unlock.summary: Confirming by sliding all the way to the end.
slide-to-unlock.description: Slide to unlock runs only after the handle is slid to the end of its track. Early phone lock screens used it to prevent accidental taps in a pocket. Released before the end, the handle returns to the start.

reduced-motion.summary: An alternative for people who reduce motion.
reduced-motion.description: For people who turned on reduced motion on their device, the same change is shown with a short fade instead of a large movement. Motion isn't removed but made gentler, and the message stays the same.

page-transition.summary: A transition that shows where the new screen came from.
page-transition.description: A page transition slides in from the side when going from a list to its details and moves the opposite way going back, showing which screen comes first. Unrelated screens fade through, and temporary screens rise from the bottom as a modal.

expand-collapse-motion.summary: A card that grows in place to reveal more.
expand-collapse-motion.description: Expand/collapse motion grows a folded card downward in place to show its details when pressed. Changing grid-template-rows from 0fr to 1fr opens it to the real content height without measuring it.

micro-interaction.summary: A small, quick response at the moment of a press.
micro-interaction.description: A micro-interaction is a small response to a single action, such as a save icon that dips, pops, and fills when pressed. It finishes within 300ms, and the result also stays as an icon and words, so missing the motion loses nothing.

shake-on-error.summary: Shaking a wrong input side to side.
shake-on-error.description: Shake on error wiggles a field briefly side to side, like shaking a head, when a password is wrong. The shake is only emphasis, so a red border and an error message appear with it.

shared-element-transition.summary: A thumbnail that grows into the detail screen.
shared-element-transition.description: A shared element transition grows a photo from a list into the large photo on the detail screen. The View Transitions API links elements with the same name on both screens; browsers without it simply switch screens.

scroll-reveal.summary: Appearing as it scrolls into view.
scroll-reveal.description: Scroll reveal makes content rise slightly or grow into place the moment it enters the screen. IntersectionObserver plays it once on first view, and content is shown from the start where observing isn't supported.

parallax.summary: A background that moves at a different speed.
parallax.description: Parallax moves the picture behind more slowly than the text in front while scrolling, adding depth. Writing the scroll position straight into the style, instead of re-rendering state, keeps it smooth; with reduced motion, everything scrolls together.

ease-in-out.summary: Easing that shapes the speed at the start and end.
ease-in-out.description: Easing curves keep the same distance and time but move slowly at the start, at the end, or at both. Entering elements look natural with ease-out, leaving ones with ease-in, and ones moving between places with ease-in-out.

fade.description: A fade is the calmest transition: only opacity changes as an element appears or disappears. Appearing uses CSS @starting-style, and the element is removed only after the exit transition ends.

slide.description: A slide brings an element in from one edge and takes it out the same way. Because it comes and goes in the same direction, people know where it's tucked away.

spring.summary: Overshooting the target, coming back, and settling.
spring.description: A spring overshoots its target a little, comes back, and settles, like a weight on a spring. It's defined by stiffness and friction instead of duration, so if the target changes mid-motion, it keeps its speed and turns naturally.

bounce.summary: Hitting the ground and bouncing back up.
bounce.description: A bounce moves like a ball dropped on the floor, bouncing lower each time until it stops. When a product goes into the cart, the cart hops once and draws the eye to where the number changed.

stagger.summary: Showing several elements one after another at short intervals.
stagger.description: Stagger brings list items up one after another from the top instead of all at once. Keep the gap to tens of milliseconds per item and finish the whole sequence within 400ms.

zoom-transition.summary: A screen growing out of its icon.
zoom-transition.description: A zoom transition grows a screen out of the app icon that was pressed and shrinks it back into the icon on close. Setting transform-origin to the pressed position shows where the screen came from.

count-up.summary: A number that counts up and settles.
count-up.description: Count up raises a key figure quickly from zero and slows to a stop at the end. It draws the eye to a big number, while screen readers hear only the final number from the start.

typewriter.summary: A sentence typed out one letter at a time.
typewriter.description: A typewriter effect writes a sentence one letter at a time with a blinking cursor at the end. It suggests someone speaking right now, as in a chat assistant's greeting.

rotating-words.summary: Words taking turns in one spot.
rotating-words.description: Rotating words lift the last word of a sentence out at a fixed interval and bring the next one up. One sentence shows several uses, and a pause button stops it at any time.

marquee.summary: A strip that scrolls sideways without end.
marquee.description: A marquee scrolls short phrases such as free shipping or ships today endlessly sideways in a strip. The list is repeated twice for a seamless loop, and it pauses on hover or with a pause button.

text-scramble.summary: Letters that scramble and then settle.
text-scramble.description: Text scramble cycles quickly through symbols and settles into the real letters one by one from the left. It stages the moment something is processed and a result appears, as in connecting or decoding.

staggered-text-reveal.summary: Lines or words appearing at intervals.
staggered-text-reveal.description: A staggered text reveal brings the lines or words of a heading up from below at short intervals. Appearing in reading order brings out the rhythm of the sentence.

fade-up.summary: Text that rises as it comes into focus.
fade-up.description: Fade up is the safest entrance: text rises about 10px from below as it goes from transparent to solid. Showing the heading, body, and button slightly later each guides the reading order.

animated-highlight.summary: A highlighter stroke across the key phrase.
animated-highlight.description: An animated highlight paints a highlighter behind the key phrase of a sentence from left to right. It paints once on first view, and because it's a real mark element, the emphasis stays even without motion.

mask-reveal.summary: Text rising out from behind a mask.
mask-reveal.description: A mask reveal hides each line below an invisible edge and slides it up into view. Each line starts one line-height down inside an overflow-hidden box.

blur-in.description: Blur in brings faint, blurry text into focus. It gives a short sentence a calm, refined feel; the blur filter is expensive, so use it on a single heading line.

bar-chart.summary: Comparing sizes across categories by length.
bar-chart.description: A bar chart compares split categories such as weekdays or regions by bar length starting at zero. Names and values are written as text so it reads without the bars, and bars ease to their new length when the data changes.

line-chart.summary: Following how a value changes along an ordered axis.
line-chart.description: A line chart shows with a 2px line how values change along an ordered axis such as months or weeks. Moving the guide line with the pointer or the left and right arrows reads every series at that point in one line, and series names sit at the line ends and in the legend.

donut-chart.summary: The share of each part of a whole.
donut-chart.description: A donut chart shows the share of a few parts of a whole as ring segments. The total sits in the middle and changes to a part's share when its segment or legend entry is pointed at. The legend lists values and percentages, and "other" stays gray.

sparkline.summary: A small trend line inside a card or table.
sparkline.description: A sparkline shows a trend as a line the size of text, with no axes or ticks. It fits in a table cell or card next to a number, with a dot on the last value; exact values sit beside it as text.

gauge.summary: The current value in a range, with a target.
gauge.description: A gauge shows where the current value sits in a fixed range as a half-circle bar. A target, if any, is marked on the scale, and the value and range are also written as text. The bar grows smoothly when the value changes.

heatmap.summary: Showing where values cluster by color depth in a grid.
heatmap.description: A heatmap shades cells where two dimensions meet, such as weekday and hour, in depths of one color to show where values cluster. Pointing at a cell or moving with the arrows outlines it and reads the exact value, with a color scale legend below.

kpi-card.summary: A key metric and its change against a comparison period.
kpi-card.description: A KPI card shows one key number large on a dashboard together with its change and what it's compared with. An arrow, a sign, and the words up or down show the direction, and the color depends on whether the change is good or bad for that metric.

stacked-bar-chart.summary: Comparing totals and their makeup within bars.
stacked-bar-chart.description: A stacked bar chart splits each bar into parts in the same order to show the total and its makeup together. As counts, bar length compares totals; as percentages, equal-length bars compare composition. Parts are separated by 2px gaps and show their values on hover.

column-chart.summary: Comparing ordered categories by vertical bar height.
column-chart.description: A column chart compares ordered categories such as months or quarters by vertical bar height from zero. The scale stays the same when the period changes, so heights stay comparable, and pointing at a bar shows its value.

pie-chart.summary: The share of a few parts of a whole.
pie-chart.description: A pie chart divides a circle into slices by each part's share. Large slices carry their percentage directly, and the legend lists values and percentages. Pointing at a slice or legend entry leaves only that part at full strength.

venn-diagram.summary: Where two or three sets overlap, and the count in each region.
venn-diagram.description: A Venn diagram overlaps two or three circles and writes the count in each region the overlaps create. The circles stay the same size so the numbers tell the size; choosing a set in the legend highlights its circle and reads its total.

bubble-chart.summary: Comparing three values by position and circle size.
bubble-chart.description: A bubble chart places circles by two values and sizes their area by a third, comparing many items at once. Circles overlap semi-transparently with white outlines, and the one pointed at comes to the front and reads its values.

radar-chart.summary: Comparing strengths across several measures around a circle.
radar-chart.description: A radar chart places several measures on the same scale as axes around a circle and joins the values into a shape. The shape shows strengths and weaknesses at a glance, and two shapes overlaid show where two subjects differ.

scatter-plot.summary: The relationship between two values, and outliers.
scatter-plot.description: A scatter plot places dots by two values, one across and one up, to see whether they grow together and which dots stand apart. Pointing anywhere reads the nearest dot, and turning on the average lines splits the plot into four quadrants.

area-chart.summary: Amounts over time as the area under a line.
area-chart.description: An area chart fills under a line lightly to stress how much there is over time. It's drawn on an axis starting at zero, and moving the guide line with the pointer or the left and right arrows reads that day's value.

histogram.summary: The shape of a distribution in equal-width bins.
histogram.description: A histogram splits many values into bins of equal width and shows how many fall in each as bars. The bins are continuous, so the bars touch, and changing the bin width shows how the same data can take different shapes.

treemap.summary: Comparing sizes by dividing a rectangle by area.
treemap.description: A treemap divides a rectangle into smaller rectangles by each item's value. Laying out large items first, close to square, makes areas easy to compare, and roomy cells carry their name and value directly.

waterfall-chart.summary: Stacking increases and decreases in order up to the result.
waterfall-chart.description: A waterfall chart starts from an opening value, stacks increases and decreases in turn as floating bars, and ends with the result. From revenue to net profit, it shows at a glance how much each item moved the result.

box-plot.summary: Summarizing a distribution with the median, the middle 50%, and the range.
box-plot.description: A box plot draws each group's middle half as a box, its median as a line, its usual range as whiskers, and anything far outside as dots. It compares spread and skew across groups side by side, which an average alone can't show.

bullet-chart.summary: One metric against a target line and rating bands.
bullet-chart.description: A bullet chart overlays the current value, a target line, and poor, fair, and good bands on a single bar. It takes less room than a gauge, so many metrics stack well, and the value and target are also written as text.

waffle-chart.summary: Showing a share as counts in a 100-cell grid.
waffle-chart.description: A waffle chart fills cells of a 10×10 grid, each worth 1%. It reads as counts, such as 68 out of 100 people, which works for people who find percentages unfamiliar, and the legend lists every share as text.

calendar-heatmap.summary: Daily values as shading in calendar cells.
calendar-heatmap.description: A calendar heatmap lays a month or a year out in cells by weekday and week and shades each day's value in depths of one color. Consistency and weekly rhythms in things like exercise or journaling stand out, and pointing at a cell or moving with the arrows reads that day's value.

slope-chart.summary: Increases, decreases, and rank changes between two points in time.
slope-chart.description: A slope chart plots each item's values at two points in time on two vertical lines and joins them. Rising, falling, and crossing lines show changes and rank shifts at once, and pointing at an item fades the rest.

polar-area-chart.summary: Cyclical values as slice lengths at equal angles.
polar-area-chart.description: A polar area chart divides a circle into equal angles and extends each slice outward by its value. For data that cycles, such as months or hours, it shows when values cluster; the radius grows with the square root so slice area matches the value.

empty-state.summary: Explaining why there's nothing to show and what to do next.
empty-state.description: An empty state doesn't leave a blank space when a list or search has no results; it explains why it's empty and what people can do next.

error-state.summary: Explaining a failed load and how to recover.
error-state.description: When the request for a list or detail screen fails, an error state says which task ran into a problem and lets people try again on the same screen.

no-results.summary: An empty result that helps people change their query.
no-results.description: When a search finds nothing, no results shows what was searched and suggests similar terms and fixes, so people search again instead of leaving a blank screen.

offline-state.summary: What to show when the connection drops.
offline-state.description: An offline state explains what's wrong when the network connection drops and says the content will reload on its own once connected. A button lets people retry themselves.

not-found-page.summary: A way back when the address is wrong.
not-found-page.description: A 404 page explains in plain words what happened when people land on an address that doesn't exist, and offers a way on through search or the home page. The next step comes before the error code.

permission-denied.summary: Why something can't be viewed and how to ask for access.
permission-denied.description: Permission denied explains why people can't see what they opened and how to get access. It shows who can grant it and which account they're signed in with, and leads straight to a request.

maintenance-page.description: A maintenance page says when planned maintenance started, when it ends, and how long is left while the service is unavailable. People can ask to be notified when it's over, so they don't have to keep refreshing.

no-filter-results.summary: An empty result that shows the filters in use and suggests loosening them.
no-filter-results.description: When too many filters leave no results, this shows the filters in use and lets people remove them one by one or clear them all in place, so they can fix whichever condition emptied the list.

all-caught-up.summary: Saying there's nothing left to do and no new notifications.
all-caught-up.description: When every notification or task is handled and the list is empty, all caught up says the work is done instead of feeling like something is missing. It also says when and where new items will appear.

emptied-state.summary: What happens after the last item is removed, and what to do next.
emptied-state.description: When removing the last item empties a list, an emptied state says what was just removed and offers undo and a next action. Unlike a list that started empty, it makes clear this is the result of what people just did.

locked-content.summary: The terms for access and how to unlock it.
locked-content.description: Locked content shows only the beginning of something that needs a membership or payment and says what's needed to see the rest. Previewing what people will get helps them decide.

onboarding-carousel.summary: A service introduction to swipe through.
onboarding-carousel.description: An onboarding carousel introduces the core of a service in three or four screens, one at a time, to people opening the app for the first time. Skip is always visible, it never advances on its own, and the last screen's button becomes Get started.

coach-mark.summary: A one-time hint pointing at a button.
coach-mark.description: A coach mark dims the rest of the screen, lights up one button, and explains its use in a short bubble. It shows only the first time and disappears once acknowledged.

product-tour.summary: Pointing out parts of the screen in several steps.
product-tour.description: A product tour lights up and explains the main features of a screen, such as search, filters, and export, one at a time. It shows which step people are on, and they can stop at any time with previous, next, or skip.

setup-checklist.summary: A first to-do list with progress.
setup-checklist.description: A setup checklist shows the first things to do as a list of about four items with a progress bar. Each item has a button to start it, and finished items are checked in place so the list doesn't shift.

permission-priming.summary: Explaining why a permission is needed before the system asks.
permission-priming.description: Permission priming is the app's own screen explaining why it needs notifications, location, or the camera before the device asks. It appears at the moment of need, such as right after an order, and choosing Later skips the system prompt to save that one chance.

welcome-screen.summary: A first-visit greeting and a start button.
welcome-screen.description: A welcome modal greets first-time visitors with one sentence about what the service does and a start button. People can choose to look around first, and closing it with Esc counts as looking around.

whats-new.description: What's new shows up to three changes in plain words, once, right after an update. After it's closed, a news button shows it again.

splash-screen.summary: The screen shown while an app gets ready.
splash-screen.description: A splash screen shows the logo while the app opens and moves straight to home when it's ready. It stays a minimum time so it doesn't flash, but never holds people once everything is ready.

social-sign-in.summary: Signing up and signing in with an outside account.
social-sign-in.description: Social sign-in is a set of buttons for signing up and signing in at once with an account people already have. Each button names its account in words, and only the pressed one shows it's connecting while the rest wait, so nothing starts twice.

terms-agreement.summary: A consent screen that separates required and optional terms.
terms-agreement.description: A terms agreement lists required and optional terms under Agree to all, and people can continue only after checking every required one. Checking some shows Agree to all in an in-between state, and each term can be opened to read.

profile-setup.summary: Choosing a nickname and photo for the first time.
profile-setup.description: Profile setup is the step right after sign-up for choosing a nickname and photo. Before a photo is picked, it shows the nickname's first letter; it states the length rule before typing, and people can skip with Later.

system-permission-dialog.summary: The step where the device takes the permission decision.
system-permission-dialog.description: A system permission dialog is the window the device itself shows after the app explains why. The app can't change its look, only its message, so write one exact sentence about what the permission is for, and prepare the next screen for each outcome.

permission-recovery.summary: A way to turn it back on after a refusal, and an alternative.
permission-recovery.description: Permission recovery says what won't work after a refusal and offers Allow again if the device can still ask, or Open settings if it can't. A way to continue without the permission, such as typing an address, sits beside it.

limited-access.summary: Using only the allowed scope and changing it when needed.
limited-access.description: When people allow only part of something, such as a few photos, limited access draws the screen from that scope and says so in one line. If more is needed, they can change the selection right there.

success-screen.summary: The result and next steps after payment or sign-up.
success-screen.description: A success screen announces the result with a clear heading right after payment or sign-up, along with the details people want to check at once, such as the order number and amount, and the next actions. Focus moves to the heading so screen reader users hear the result right away.

success-checkmark.description: A success checkmark fills a circle and then draws a check in one stroke. Use it briefly for a success people waited for, such as a money transfer, and state the result in words too.

confetti.summary: Paper pieces at the moment a goal is reached.
confetti.description: Confetti bursts once and scatters at the moment a long goal is reached, such as walking for 30 days. It's decoration only, so screen readers skip it, and a message about the achievement appears with it.

receipt-summary.description: A receipt summary puts the amount paid and the payment method at the top and lets people expand the items with one press. Amounts align right with fixed-width digits, and discounts show a minus sign along with color.

streak.summary: A count of how many days in a row.
streak.description: A streak shows how many days in a row something has continued and marks this week's recorded days. Recording today makes the number hop once to show it went up.

achievement-badge.summary: Locked before earning, the moment of earning, and a shelf of badges.
achievement-badge.description: A locked achievement badge shows the remaining progress (4/5) with a ring, and fills with color and shows the date when earned. Locked goals aren't hidden, so people know what to do next.

completed-task-strikethrough.description: When a task is checked, a line draws across its text from the left and it turns gray. The checkbox holds the real state; the line is a visual that adds the feeling of being done.

completion-stamp.description: A completion stamp presses down on a finished mission card or coupon at a slight angle. It comes down slightly large and settles in place like ink on paper, and completion is also stated in words.

send-animation.summary: Marking the moment of sending with a short motion.
send-animation.description: A send animation flies a paper plane up to the right when Send is pressed, brings a new one back, and raises the sent message at the bottom of the conversation. The motion is only a signal; the result stays as a message in the conversation.

star-rating.summary: Rating with whole or half stars.
star-rating.description: A star rating takes a score with five stars. Underneath it's a native radio group, so the arrow keys move the score, and when half steps are needed, each star's left and right halves can be pressed separately.

like-button.description: A like button leaves a public reaction with a heart and updates the count at once. It applies the change before the server responds and reverts if it fails, and the heart pops only when turned on.

share-sheet.description: A share sheet opens the device's share window (navigator.share) when the share button is pressed, and a small sheet with copy link, message, and email in browsers without it. The icon follows the platform: a box and arrow on iOS, three dots on Android.

emoji-reaction.summary: Reacting with one of several feelings.
emoji-reaction.description: Emoji reactions place chips with an emoji and a count under a message, and pressing one adds or removes your reaction. A plus button opens a small picker for a new reaction.

thumbs-feedback.summary: Rating whether it helped with yes or no.
thumbs-feedback.description: Thumbs feedback asks at the end of a help article whether it helped. Yes ends with a thank-you, and only No shows reason chips, so most people answer in one tap.

rating-summary.summary: An average and distribution bars by score.
rating-summary.description: A rating summary shows the average score, the total number of reviews, and distribution bars by score. Pressing a bar filters reviews to that score, and each bar has its count in text so it reads without the graphic.

copy-link.summary: Copying an address and confirming it.
copy-link.description: Copy link places a read-only address field beside a copy button. Copying also selects the address, so people can copy it by hand if the clipboard is blocked, and the result is announced for two seconds.

nps-scale.summary: Asking how likely people are to recommend, from 0 to 10.
nps-scale.description: An NPS scale asks how likely people are to recommend something to a friend on a scale of 0 to 10. All scores look the same before a choice so none is nudged, and only one follow-up question matching the score is asked.

invite-dialog.summary: Inviting people to work together by email.
invite-dialog.description: An invite dialog turns an email address into a removable chip when people press Enter or a comma. Malformed addresses don't become chips and show an error, and the send button says how many people are being invited.

mention.description: A mention input lists matching people when @ is typed in a comment and inserts @name for the one chosen. Focus stays in the field while the list is open, so typing can continue.

comment-thread.description: A comment thread indents replies one level under each comment. Replies fold behind "View 2 replies", and pressing Reply opens a field right under that comment.

emoji-rating.description: An emoji rating takes satisfaction with five faces in order, from frowning to smiling. Each face has a word name from very dissatisfied to very satisfied, so its meaning is clear without reading the face.

written-review.summary: Writing about an experience along with a star rating.
written-review.description: A written review form takes a star rating and a review together. It shows the length rule and current character count while people type, and on submit it checks the form and moves focus to the first problem.

rating-slider.summary: Entering a satisfaction score within a range.
rating-slider.description: A rating slider picks a score by dragging along a range from 0 to 10. The current score floats above the handle, and words under both ends show which way the numbers go.

rating-tags.summary: Choosing reasons along with a star rating.
rating-tags.description: Rating tags let people press reason chips such as Friendly or Fast after choosing a star rating. High scores show what went well and low scores what fell short, and writing stays optional.

rating-badge.summary: A rating and review count summed up on a card.
rating-badge.description: A rating badge adds one star, the rating, and the review count to a card or list. Showing the count tells a 4.9 from 7 reviews apart from a 4.6 from 1,284.

wishlist-bookmark.summary: Saving items to your own list to see later.
wishlist-bookmark.description: A wishlist or bookmark toggle saves a product or post to a list only you see. Unlike a public like, it goes into your list, so it shows the list count and a short confirmation.

qr-sharing.summary: Passing a link through a code read by a camera.
qr-sharing.description: QR sharing shows a code that opens a link when someone nearby scans it with a camera. A small encoder for short links lives inside the component, with no library, and the address is also shown as text for people who can't scan.

send-forward.summary: Passing an existing item to someone else.
send-forward.description: Send/forward is a picker for sending a photo or message to other people in the app. People search by name, check several, add a note, and send with a button that says how many will receive it.

repost.summary: Sharing an existing post again in your feed.
repost.description: Pressing repost opens a menu with two choices: repost as is, or quote it with your own words. If it's already reposted, the same menu undoes it.

nearby-share.summary: Sending straight to a nearby device.
nearby-share.description: Nearby share lists devices one by one as they're found, waits for the other person to accept once one is chosen, and then reports whether it was sent or declined. The operating system does the discovery; this component is the screen that shows its results.

chat-interface.description: A chat interface stacks your messages in bubbles on the right and replies on the left. It follows new messages only when people are at the bottom; if they scrolled up to read, it holds its place and shows a new messages button.

streaming-text.summary: An answer that arrives as if being written.
streaming-text.description: Streaming text shows an answer a few characters at a time as it's generated, with a cursor at the end. While writing, it stays aria-busy so screen readers don't read every fragment, and stopping keeps what was written so far.

prompt-input.summary: An input with attachments and send or stop.
prompt-input.description: A prompt input is where people write a question, growing up to a few lines as the text gets longer. Enter sends and Shift+Enter adds a line, and while an answer is being generated, the send button turns into a stop button in the same spot.

suggested-prompts.summary: Examples you press to ask right away.
suggested-prompts.description: Suggested prompts show a few example questions about what the assistant does well while the conversation is empty. Pressing one sends it at once, so people who don't know what to ask can learn by trying.

thinking-indicator.summary: Showing that an answer is being prepared.
thinking-indicator.description: A thinking indicator moves three dots up and down where the reply bubble will be, saying the assistant is thinking. After three seconds, it also shows the elapsed time so it doesn't look stuck.

response-feedback.description: Response feedback is a row of icons under an answer: copy, good answer, poor answer, and regenerate. Good and poor are mutually exclusive toggles, so pressing one again undoes it.

citation.summary: Links to the sources behind an answer.
citation.description: Citations put numbers after sentences in an answer and show the source title, site, and a link to the original when pressed. The numbers match the source list under the answer, so either side leads to the evidence.

model-picker.description: A model picker shows the current model's name on a small button that opens a menu with a one-line note on when to use each model. Saying what each is for, rather than listing names, makes the choice easier.

regenerate-response.summary: Generating a new answer and comparing it with the previous one.
regenerate-response.description: Regenerate response creates a new answer to the same question without discarding the previous one, and people move between them with ‹ 1 / 2 ›. Since the earlier answer they liked isn't lost, they can try again freely.

edit-prompt.summary: Fixing a sent question and asking again from that point.
edit-prompt.description: Edit prompt lets people fix a question they already sent, in place. Pressing edit turns the bubble into an input; sending answers again from that question onward, and a line says so.

file-attachment.summary: Attaching material to send, checking it, or removing it.
file-attachment.description: File attachments show files to send with a question as chips above the input. Each shows its name, size, and upload progress, can be removed before sending, and explains right on the chip why a file can't be sent.

agent-steps.summary: Work in progress and finished steps, in order.
agent-steps.description: Agent steps show what an agent is doing as ordered steps. Finished steps have a check and a one-line result, the current step a spinner, and the rest are dimmed, so people can see how far it has come.

pricing-plan-comparison.summary: Plans side by side with total price, billing cycle, and benefits.
pricing-plan-comparison.description: A pricing plan comparison uses the same rows and price units for every plan so cost and benefits can be compared quickly. It keeps the recommended mark separate from the actual selected state.

strikethrough-price.summary: Showing the reference price next to the price you'll pay.
strikethrough-price.description: A strikethrough price shows the amount to pay next to the reference price with a line through it. The conditions of the discount can be checked right beside the price.

discount-badge.summary: A discount rate calculated from a verified reference price.
discount-badge.description: A discount badge calculates the rate from a reference price the product actually sold at and the current price. It says which price the percentage is based on, and isn't shown at all without a reference price.

countdown.summary: Time left until the real end time.
countdown.description: A countdown shows the time left until a fixed end time, by the second. It states the end date and time along with what's left, and when time runs out it says the offer has ended instead of starting over.

coupon-claim.summary: A card for claiming a coupon after seeing its terms.
coupon-claim.description: A coupon claim card writes the discount and its conditions right on the coupon and lets people claim it with one button. Afterward, the button changes to Claimed and can't be pressed again, and it says where to use it.

bundle-deal.summary: Showing from how many items, and by how much, the price drops.
bundle-deal.description: A bundle deal is a quantity picker that calculates right away when the bundle discount starts and what the price becomes. Below the threshold, it says how many more to add; once it applies, the original total is shown struck through.

low-stock-indicator.summary: Stating the real remaining stock and sold-out status.
low-stock-indicator.description: A low stock indicator shows in stock, the number left, or sold out based on the real stock of the chosen option. It shows a number only when few are left, and when sold out, it offers what people can do next, such as a restock alert, instead of buying.

lowest-price-label.summary: A lowest price that states its comparison period and scope.
lowest-price-label.description: A lowest price label lets people check which period and scope the comparison covers. The badge stays short, and pressing See basis expands the comparison period and conditions.

reward-points.summary: Points to be earned and when they're paid.
reward-points.description: Reward points show the points to be earned, calculated from the amount and the earning rate. Choices that change the rate, such as the payment method, update the amount at once, and it states when points are paid and where they can't be used.

free-shipping-progress.summary: How much more until free shipping.
free-shipping-progress.description: A free shipping progress bar shows how much the cart is short of the free shipping threshold, as an amount and a bar. The amount shrinks with each item added, and past the threshold it changes to free shipping.

search-suggestions.summary: Suggesting completions for the query being typed.
search-suggestions.description: Search suggestions list possible completions while people type in the search box. The typed part stays as is and only the added part is bold, and nothing is preselected, so Enter always searches exactly what was typed.

recent-searches.description: Recent searches list past queries, newest first, when the search box opens. Pressing one runs it again, and each has a remove button alongside Clear all, so people manage their own history.

trending-searches.summary: Popular searches, with the period they cover.
trending-searches.description: Trending searches rank queries that are popular or rising. They state when and over what period they were counted, and rank changes are shown with a symbol and also as text for screen readers.

search-filters.summary: Narrowing results with conditions and summing up the ones applied.
search-filters.description: Search filters narrow results by conditions such as price and color. The result count updates as soon as something is chosen, and applied conditions gather as chips above the results to remove one by one or all at once.

search-sort.summary: Reordering results by relevance or price.
search-sort.description: Search sort is a menu button that changes the order of search results. The button shows the current order, and the menu lists the choices with a check on the current one. Choosing one closes the menu and re-sorts the list.

search-term-highlight.summary: Marking the parts of a result that match the query.
search-term-highlight.description: Search term highlight marks the parts of a result that match the query. Each space-separated word is matched separately and case doesn't matter, and the text itself isn't changed, so it reads the same.

search-scope-tabs.summary: Switching the search scope between all, products, and brands.
search-scope-tabs.description: Search scope tabs change where the same query looks. Each tab shows its result count so people know where results are, and the query stays the same when they switch.

login-form.summary: Signing in with an email and password.
login-form.description: A login form signs people in with an email and password. A wrong attempt gets a single message that doesn't reveal which field was wrong, and show password, stay signed in, and forgot password sit together.

signup-form.summary: Sign-up that flags taken emails and password rules early.
signup-form.description: A signup form creates an account with a name, email, and password. An email that's already registered is flagged as soon as people leave the field, password rules show before typing and tick off as they're met, and entered values stay if submitting fails.

email-verification.summary: A waiting screen that says where the email went and how to resend it.
email-verification.description: Email verification is the screen for waiting on the verification email after sign-up. It says which address it went to and what to check if it doesn't arrive, and lets people resend after a short wait or fix a mistyped address.

password-reset.summary: A reset request that doesn't reveal who has an account.
password-reset.description: Password reset sends a reset link to the registered email. An unregistered address gets the same reply, so this screen can't be used to find out who's a member. It also says how long the link is valid.

two-factor-auth.summary: Checking once more with a one-time code after the password.
two-factor-auth.description: Two-factor authentication asks for a code sent to the phone after the password. A code from a text message fills itself in, a wrong code shows the attempts left, and a backup code gets people in if they lose their phone.

account-deletion.summary: Deletion that shows what's lost and confirms by typing.
