account-deletion.description: Account deletion shows what goes away with the account, asks optionally why people are leaving, and enables the button only after a set word is typed. Once requested, it says until when it can be undone.

cart.summary: A cart that totals only the products you selected.
cart.description: A cart lists saved products where people choose what to buy this time, change quantities, and remove items. The total and the order button count only the selected products, so the amount to pay is always visible.

checkout-summary.summary: The amounts that make up the total and the required consent, in one place.
checkout-summary.description: A checkout summary shows the item total, shipping, and discounts line by line right before payment, with the final amount large. Discounts show as subtracted amounts, the pay button repeats the final amount, and it turns on only after required consent.

address-form.summary: Searching and choosing an address, then typing only the details.
address-form.description: An address form lets people search by street or building name, choose from the list, and type only the unit details. Choosing an address moves focus straight to the details field, and it can be saved as the default address.

payment-method.summary: Payment methods that expand only the options the chosen one needs.
payment-method.description: Payment method lets people choose card, wallet, or bank transfer as large radio cards. Options only one method needs, such as installments, expand inside its card only when that method is chosen.

order-tracking.summary: Delivery status with times for past steps and the current step.
order-tracking.description: Order tracking shows the steps from payment to delivery as an ordered list. Past steps keep their times and the current step is marked, with the expected delivery date and tracking number at the top to read and copy right away.

order-cancellation.summary: Cancellation that calculates the refund in advance.
order-cancellation.description: Order cancellation lets people choose the items to cancel and a reason, then calculates the expected refund before they submit. It also lists discounts taken back because coupon conditions no longer hold, and how the refund is paid.

settings-list.summary: Settings that combine instant switches and rows that lead to another screen.
settings-list.description: A settings list groups settings by topic, such as notifications, display, and account. Switches apply the moment they're pressed, rows with values show the current value and lead to a chooser, and risky rows such as delete account sit at the bottom in a different color.

notification-settings.summary: A table for choosing notifications by topic and channel.
notification-settings.description: Notification settings put topics such as orders, events, and comments in rows and app push, email, and text in columns, so people pick only the combinations they want. Required notifications are checked and locked with the reason, and quiet hours sit alongside.

theme-switcher.summary: Three choices that say what the system setting is right now.
theme-switcher.description: A theme switcher offers system, light, and dark as preview cards. When system is chosen, it also says which one is showing now, so people see the result of their choice at once.

language-picker.summary: A list that writes each language in itself and finds it in any language.
language-picker.description: A language picker writes each language's name in that language, with its name in the current language beside it. Searching works with either name, so people can find their way back even after switching to a language they can't read.

privacy-settings.summary: Settings that say who sees what at each level and let you get your data.
privacy-settings.description: Privacy settings describe in one line who can actually see a profile for each visibility choice. Detailed switches such as appearing in search sit alongside a button to request a copy of your data.

connected-accounts.summary: Account links that won't let you remove the last sign-in method.
connected-accounts.description: Connected accounts list outside accounts used for sign-in, such as Kakao and Google, to connect and disconnect. When an account has no password and only one connection, the disconnect button is locked with the reason, so people can't lose every way into their account by mistake.

type-to-confirm.summary: A delete button that turns on only after typing the name.
type-to-confirm.description: Type to confirm shows what goes away before an irreversible delete and turns the button on only after the exact name of the target is typed. It makes people read and think once more than a confirm button pressed out of habit.

trash.summary: A place where deleted items can be restored for a set time.
trash.description: Trash holds deleted items for a set period instead of removing them at once. Each item shows the days until permanent deletion, items about to go are also marked with color, and Restore puts an item back where it was in one step.

autosave-indicator.summary: Saying the save status in one line instead of a save button.
autosave-indicator.description: An autosave indicator shows in one line beside the editor whether the content is saved. It says saving while people type and just saved when done, and if the connection drops it says the work is saved on this device only, so people don't have to wonder whether they can leave.

unsaved-changes.summary: Asking before leaving only when something changed.
unsaved-changes.description: An unsaved changes warning asks only when people try to leave without saving changes. Save and leave, Leave without saving, and Keep editing are named by their result, and when nothing changed it leaves without asking.

bulk-actions.summary: Acting on several items at once while showing how many are selected.
bulk-actions.description: Bulk actions show an action bar with the number selected once items in a list are chosen. Even large actions such as delete report how many were handled, with undo right beside, so they can run without asking first.

version-history.summary: Previewing an old version and restoring it as a new one.
version-history.description: Version history lists saved versions, newest first, with who changed what. Choosing an older version previews it, and restoring stacks that content on top as a new version, so the current content stays in the record too.

session-timeout.summary: A warning that shows the time left and extends it in one step.
session-timeout.description: A session timeout warning shows the time left and an extend button before a sign-in ends from inactivity. After a sign-out, it says whether the work in progress was saved, and signing in again lets people pick up where they left off.

resume-prompt.summary: Showing where you stopped and your progress, and continuing at once.
resume-prompt.description: A resume prompt is a card that tells returning people what they were doing and how far they got, and continues with one button. It shows the progress, and keeps the choices to start over or close.
aliases: pick up where you left off

subscription-cancellation.summary: Cancellation that states the end date first and finishes on one screen.
subscription-cancellation.description: Subscription cancellation first shows until when the service keeps working and what changes after that, and then finishes the cancellation on one screen. Giving a reason is optional, and pausing is offered only as a choice side by side with canceling.

dormant-account.summary: A notice saying which account went dormant, when, and what was kept.
dormant-account.description: A dormant account notice appears when people sign in to an account that went dormant after long disuse. It says which account, when it went dormant, and which points and order history were kept aside, and reactivates it in one step.

update-prompt.summary: Telling updates that can wait apart from ones that can't.
update-prompt.description: An update prompt briefly shows what's new in a version. An optional update offers Later; a required update replaces the close button with why it's needed, so people know what's blocking them.

flat-design.description: Flat design drops shadows, textures, and depth effects and builds the screen from solid planes and clear color contrast. It spread on mobile screens in the early 2010s; every design style entry draws the same playlist card so the differences can be compared.

material-design.description: Material Design treats screen elements as sheets of paper at different heights and uses shadow size to show which is above which. A pressed button grows its shadow as if lifting slightly, and buttons use uppercase letters with wide spacing.

glassmorphism.description: Glassmorphism makes a translucent surface look like frosted glass by blurring the background behind it. backdrop-filter blurs what's behind, and a thin white border draws the edge of the glass.

neumorphism.summary: Soft surfaces that bulge out or sink in.
neumorphism.description: Neumorphism gives a surface the same color as the background both a light and a dark shadow, so it seems to bulge softly or press in. A pressed button switches to an inner shadow and looks sunken.

skeuomorphism.description: Skeuomorphism imitates the materials and light of real objects such as leather, metal, and vinyl records. Glossy, raised buttons and shadows that sink when pressed make it feel like handling a real thing.

claymorphism.description: Claymorphism makes elements look like soft clay toys with large rounded corners, a bright inner light, and colored outer shadows. Unlike neumorphism, surfaces are colored, so their edges are easy to see.

brutalism.description: Brutalism strips away decoration and shows the web in its raw state: default fonts, thin lines, sharp corners, and plain underlined text. Deliberately awkward placement and primary colors make a strong impression.

minimalism.summary: A screen with only what's needed.
minimalism.description: Minimalism keeps only what's essential and tidies it with generous white space, thin type, and fine lines. Even buttons shrink to an underline instead of a border, so the content comes first.

neo-brutalism.summary: Thick outlines, strong contrast, and hard shadows.
neo-brutalism.description: Neo-brutalism uses thick black outlines, hard shadows offset to the side without blur, and bright primary colors. A pressed button drops into its shadow's place, as if really pushed down.

three-d-icon.summary: Icons that show material through volume and light.
three-d-icon.description: 3D icons keep the screen flat but give the icons volume, light, and reflections so they look like something you could hold. Inner shadows, highlights, and a tinted shadow underneath create the depth.

liquid-glass.summary: A glass surface that light and color shine and bend through.
liquid-glass.description: Liquid glass is a style in which the light and color of the background show through a clear glass surface and light seems to reflect at its edges. This example approximates it with a saturated blur, a top reflection, and inner highlights; true refraction depends on platform features.

acid-graphic.summary: Near-neon colors and roughly distorted forms.
acid-graphic.description: Acid graphics use near-neon lime and magenta with stretched and slanted forms for the intensity of a 1990s rave poster. This example adds a bleeding glow and an offset colored shadow to letters stretched tall and slanted.

glitch.summary: Shifted channels and broken strokes that suggest a digital error.
glitch.description: Glitch stages a screen error by shifting the red and cyan channels and cutting away parts of the letters. The same text is layered twice more with different positions and clipped areas.

bauhaus.summary: Lettering built from geometric forms such as circles and straight lines.
bauhaus.description: Bauhaus style places basic shapes such as circles, squares, and triangles and the primary colors red, blue, and yellow together with letters. It comes from the design principles of the Bauhaus, a German design school of the 1920s.

art-deco.description: Art Deco expresses the glamour of the 1920s with tall, thin letters, wide spacing, and gold and double-line ornaments. Symmetry and repeated lines define it.

outline.summary: Shapes defined by letter outlines rather than fill.
outline.description: Outline type leaves the inside of letters empty and draws only the outline to show their shape. It's made with -webkit-text-stroke on bold letters and mixed with filled letters for contrast.

monospace.summary: Letters set at an equal width.
monospace.description: Monospace sets every letter in a cell of the same width. It feels like code, a typewriter, or a table; this example draws the cells as lines to show the fixed width.

hand-lettering.description: Hand lettering gives a warm, personal feel with handwritten strokes, slants, and underlines. This example uses a script-like font, slanted text, and a hand-drawn underline.

minimal-typography.summary: Bringing out the key phrase with space and type contrast.
minimal-typography.description: Minimal typography removes ornament and shows a phrase with only very thin, large letters and wide space. Small supporting text with wide letter spacing creates the size contrast.

brutalist-typography.summary: Huge, rough letters with hard cuts and overlaps.
brutalist-typography.description: Brutalist typography blows letters up too large and tightens the line height until they overlap, or cuts them with color bands for a strong impression. Rules are broken on purpose to create tension.

neo-brutalist-typography.summary: Thick borders and strong contrast on headings and labels.
neo-brutalist-typography.description: Neo-brutalist typography puts letters in boxes with thick black borders and unblurred shadows so they look like sticker labels. The boxes tilt slightly to feel stuck on by hand.

swiss-style.summary: Hierarchy built with a regular grid and alignment.
swiss-style.description: Swiss style sets sans-serif type flush left on a strict grid and builds hierarchy with minimal elements such as color bands. It's the International Typographic Style defined in Switzerland in the 1950s.

editorial-typography.summary: Reading order built from title and body contrast and white space.
editorial-typography.description: Editorial typography leads the reading order like a magazine with serif titles, italic subheads, rules, and space. The contrast in size and weight between title and body is the key.

chunky.summary: Heavy, thick strokes that read as a single mass.
chunky.description: Chunky type uses the heaviest weight, tight spacing, and slightly widened forms so the letters read as one block. It stands out even from far away.

retro-groovy.summary: Thick, wavy strokes and soft curves.
retro-groovy.description: Retro groovy varies each letter's height and angle like a wave, as on a 1970s poster, and layers orange and yellow shadows.

pixel-typography.summary: Stepped strokes aligned to a pixel grid.
pixel-typography.description: Pixel typography builds letters by turning on dots in a small grid, recalling old games and LED signs. This example draws the phrase as a bitmap and scales it up with SVG rectangles.

kinetic-typography.summary: Stressing a sentence's meaning or rhythm with motion and speed.
kinetic-typography.description: Kinetic typography makes letters pop up in turn or move to stress a sentence's rhythm and meaning. Motion stops with reduced motion, and screen readers get the whole phrase at once.

neon-sign.summary: Glowing tube outlines and spreading light.
neon-sign.description: Neon sign type spreads several layers of light around letters on a dark background so they look like neon tubes. A white core is layered with a pink glow.

graffiti.summary: The free strokes of handwriting and spray-painted murals.
graffiti.description: Graffiti type slants and twists letters with thick outlines and neon gradients so they look like a street mural. A brick pattern background adds context.

blackletter.summary: A typeface with angular, ornamented strokes.
blackletter.description: Blackletter is the angular, ornamental type of medieval European manuscripts. Hangul has no such form, so it's used with Latin text; this example uses Unicode mathematical Fraktur characters with a separate name for screen readers.

stencil.summary: Strokes broken in places as if sprayed through a plate.
stencil.description: Stencil type breaks strokes at regular points, as if paint were sprayed through a plate. This example cuts the strokes with a horizontal mask to create the bridges.

comic-pop-art.summary: Bold outlines, halftone dots, and comic action lines.
comic-pop-art.description: Comic pop art feels like a comic-book sound effect with thick black outlines, offset colored shadows, and a halftone dot background.

cutout-collage.summary: Mismatched letter pieces and paper textures in one phrase.
cutout-collage.description: Cutout collage mixes typefaces, colored paper, and angles for each letter so it looks clipped from magazines. Since letters are split one by one, screen readers get the whole phrase separately.

three-d-extrude.summary: Letters extended backward to show depth and sides.
three-d-extrude.description: 3D extrude stacks several layers of side faces so letters look pushed back at an angle. Shadows in the same direction, each slightly darker, are layered together.

gradient-typography.summary: Color or brightness that shifts gradually within the letters.
gradient-typography.description: Gradient typography fills letters with a gradient of several colors. It's made with background-clip: text, which cuts the background to the shape of the letters.

emboss.summary: Letters raised from the surface with light and shadow.
emboss.description: Emboss gives letters the same color as the background a bright light on one side and a dark shadow on the other, so they seem raised from the surface.

inflated-three-d.summary: Puffy, rounded 3D letters, as if filled with air.
inflated-three-d.description: Inflated 3D gives letters a round, plump volume, as if pumped with air. White outlines and shadows stacked downward express the puffed-up thickness.

chrome-typography.summary: Letters with metallic reflections and shine.
chrome-typography.description: Y2K chrome makes letters shine like metal with silver gradients and light flares. It grew popular with the Y2K aesthetic of digital optimism around the year 2000.

confirmshaming.summary: Putting guilt on the decline button.
confirmshaming.description: Confirmshaming writes the decline option as a jab, such as "No thanks, I'd rather pay full price", so people feel ashamed for saying no. The right way is to write both choices in the same tone and weight.

pre-checked-opt-in.summary: Turning on marketing consent by default.
pre-checked-opt-in.description: A pre-checked opt-in checks optional consent such as marketing messages in advance, so people who don't notice are treated as having agreed. Privacy laws often require people to turn optional consent on themselves.

roach-motel.summary: Easy to sign up, hard to cancel.
roach-motel.description: A roach motel lets people sign up with one button but makes canceling go through phone calls, many steps, and hidden menus. The right way is to let people cancel where they signed up, with the same effort, and tell them how much time they have left.

hidden-costs.summary: Charges that appear at the last step.
hidden-costs.description: Hidden costs show only a low price on the product page and add fees and shipping at the last step of checkout, so people pay a different amount than they first saw. The right way is to include every unavoidable cost in the first price shown.

fake-urgency.summary: A fake deadline that resets after it ends.
fake-urgency.description: Fake urgency shows a countdown with no real deadline, or restarts it when time runs out, to rush people. The right way is to state the real end date and time as they are.

disguised-ads.description: Disguised ads dress up as a download button or an article so people press them, mistaking them for a real feature. The right way is to label ads as ads and clearly separate them from real features in look and position.

nagging.summary: Requests that keep coming back after you close them.
nagging.description: Nagging shows requests to turn on notifications, rate the app, or sign up again on every screen after people decline, until they give in. The right way is to ask once, offer Don't ask again, and remember that choice.

sneak-into-basket.summary: Adding products or options to the cart without consent.
sneak-into-basket.description: Sneak into basket puts insurance, donations, or paid options people didn't choose into the cart in advance, so they're paid for unless noticed. The right way is to show extras as unchecked choices.

fake-scarcity.summary: Pressure to buy with stock and viewer counts that aren't real.
fake-scarcity.description: Fake scarcity rushes people with made-up numbers such as "1 left" or "37 people viewing", regardless of real stock or viewers. The right way is to show only real data, without pressuring language.

forced-continuity.summary: Turning a trial into a paid plan while hiding the terms.
forced-continuity.description: Forced continuity hides the payment terms in small print when a free trial starts and switches to a paid plan without notice when it ends. The right way is to state the billing date and amount clearly, remind people before charging, and make canceling easy.

hicks-law.description: Hick's law says that the more options there are, the longer it takes to choose one. Grouping the most-used items first and showing fewer options at once helps people choose quickly.

fitts-law.summary: Large, near buttons are easy to press.
fitts-law.description: Fitts's law says the larger and closer a target is, the faster and more accurately it can be pressed. Make frequently used main buttons large and place them where a finger or cursor reaches easily.

jakobs-law.summary: People expect things to work the way they're used to.
jakobs-law.description: Jakob's law says people spend most of their time on other services, so they expect yours to work the same way. Keeping familiar places for things like the logo, search, and cart lets people use it without learning.

von-restorff-effect.summary: The one that stands out is remembered.
von-restorff-effect.description: The Von Restorff effect says that among similar things, the one that looks different stands out and is remembered. Set apart only the one thing people must notice with color, size, or a border, and keep the rest the same.

peak-end-rule.summary: The most intense moment and the end shape the memory.
peak-end-rule.description: The peak-end rule says people remember an experience by its most intense moment and its end rather than the average of the whole. Taking care of ending screens, such as payment and delivery complete, makes the whole thing remembered well.

zeigarnik-effect.summary: Unfinished tasks keep coming to mind.
zeigarnik-effect.description: The Zeigarnik effect says unfinished tasks stay in memory longer than finished ones and make people want to wrap them up. Showing progress and what's left helps people complete settings or a profile.

choice-overload.summary: With many hard-to-compare options, people put off deciding.
choice-overload.description: Choice overload is the tendency to put off deciding when there are too many options that are hard to compare. Showing fewer options first and narrowing them with recommendations or filters makes deciding easier.

loss-aversion.summary: Losses weigh more than gains of the same size.
loss-aversion.description: Loss aversion is the tendency to feel a loss more strongly than a gain of the same size. Talk of losing works strongly, so use it to inform, not to stir up anxiety and push a decision.

default-effect.summary: The tendency to keep the preset option.
default-effect.description: People tend to keep preset values instead of changing them. A default is a decision made on their behalf, so make it the value that benefits them and is easy to undo.

social-proof.summary: Using what others do or think as a basis for judgment.
social-proof.description: Social proof is the tendency to decide by looking at what others chose when unsure. Real data such as purchase or review counts helps people decide; made-up numbers turn it into a dark pattern.

scarcity.summary: Limits on quantity or time affect choices.
scarcity.description: Scarcity is the tendency to value things more and decide faster when quantity or time is limited. Calmly stating a real limit helps people not miss out; a made-up limit becomes fake scarcity.

framing-effect.summary: The same information is judged differently depending on how it's put.
framing-effect.description: The framing effect says the same fact is received differently in a positive frame (80% fat-free) and a negative one (20% fat). For important decisions, show both frames or state the numbers plainly.

compromise-effect.summary: The middle option feels reasonable depending on the lineup.
compromise-effect.description: When the top and bottom of price and benefits change, the same plan can look like the middle option. Adding a higher plan or turning on the recommended mark lets you see separately what the lineup implies and what the label stresses.

decoy-effect.summary: Adding an inferior alternative can change relative preference.
decoy-effect.description: An option can look better when it beats an alternative with the same price and fewer benefits. In a subscription, add the comparison option and check the effect of the lineup yourself.

left-digit-effect.summary: The same difference feels larger when the leading digit changes.
left-digit-effect.description: Going from 5,800 to 5,900 won and from 5,900 to 6,000 won are both a 100 won difference. Compare price pairs where only the first digit changes.

anchoring.summary: The first number seen becomes the reference for later judgments.
anchoring.description: Anchoring says the first number presented acts like an anchor and shapes later judgments. Showing the list price first makes the sale price feel cheaper, so use only a price that something actually sold at as the reference.

hamburger.summary: Three horizontal lines that open a menu.
hamburger.description: The hamburger icon stacks three horizontal lines and opens the hidden full menu when pressed. It's named for looking like a burger's buns and patty, and usually sits at the top left on mobile.

kebab.summary: Three vertical dots for more actions on an item.
kebab.description: The kebab icon is three dots in a column, named for looking like a kebab on a skewer. It sits at the end of each row in a list and gathers actions for that item only, such as rename and delete.

meatballs.description: The meatballs icon is three dots in a row, named for looking like meatballs on a plate. It sits in a corner of a post or card and opens extra actions such as copy link and report.

bento.summary: A grid of nine squares for a list of apps.
bento.description: The bento icon places nine small squares in a 3×3 grid, named for looking like a divided lunch box. It opens a list for moving to the same company's other apps and services.

chevron.summary: An angle bracket for next or expand.
chevron.description: The chevron is a V turned on its side, named after the rank insignia on military uniforms. Pointing right means going into the next screen, left means going back, and down means expanding.

caret.summary: A small triangle for a dropdown.
caret.description: The caret is a small filled triangle, named after the proofreading mark (^) for inserting text. Next to a button label, it says pressing opens a list to choose from.

grip.summary: Six dots for dragging to move.
grip.description: The grip is a handle of six dots in two rows that means the item can be grabbed and dragged to reorder. It sits at the left of a row, keeping the grab area to the handle so the rest of the row can be pressed as usual.

sparkles.description: Sparkles show large and small four-pointed stars twinkling, now widely used to mark features where AI does the work. Placed before buttons that polish or summarize text, it says the result is generated automatically.

doner.summary: Horizontal lines of different lengths for filter and sort.
doner.description: The döner icon is three horizontal lines that get shorter from top to bottom, named after meat shaved off a döner kebab spit. It opens sorting and filtering that shrink a list or change its order.

waffle.summary: A grid of nine round dots for a list of apps.
waffle.description: The waffle icon places nine round dots in a 3×3 grid, named for looking like the hollows of a waffle. Like the bento, it opens a list for moving between apps; each service uses one or the other.

veggie-burger.summary: A menu made of two horizontal lines.
veggie-burger.description: The veggie burger icon is the hamburger with its middle line removed, named after the joke about a burger without the meat patty. It means the same as the hamburger and opens a menu, but it's less familiar, so a Menu label goes with it.

stairs.summary: Staggered horizontal lines that look like stairs.
stairs.description: The stairs icon places three horizontal lines shifted a little to the right each, like steps. It marks indented contents or menus, but its meaning is less known, so a label such as Contents goes with it.

sliders.summary: Settings and filters drawn as adjustment knobs.
sliders.description: The sliders icon draws round knobs staggered on horizontal lines, a shape taken from the faders on audio equipment. It opens filters or detailed settings for adjusting values.

user-interview.summary: Asking why people act as they do to understand the context.
user-interview.description: A user interview is a conversation with one participant about what they went through and why. Instead of questions that contain the hoped-for answer, ask them to tell a past action from the start, and the sticking points and real reasons come out.

usability-test.summary: Watching people do tasks to find where they get stuck.
usability-test.description: A usability test gives participants real tasks and observes them using the screen. Noting what they pressed and where they paused, with times, makes clear what needs fixing. Watching about five people reveals most major problems.

ab-test.summary: Comparing a chosen metric across randomly split groups.
ab-test.description: An A/B test randomly splits visitors, shows them different designs, and compares a metric chosen in advance. Decide the duration and sample size before starting and judge only after collecting that much; stopping early on a peek makes it easy to mistake chance for an effect.

card-sorting.description: Card sorting writes menu items on cards and has participants group and name them. The share of people who put cards in the same group shows the menu structure people expect.

tree-testing.summary: Checking whether people can find items in a text-only structure.
tree-testing.description: Tree testing shows only the menu structure as text, without screen design, and asks people to find the answer to a task. Success rates and the first path people took reveal where names or locations are confusing.

survey.summary: Seeing the distribution of many answers to the same questions.
survey.description: A survey asks many people the same questions to see how answers are distributed. Ask one thing per question in words that don't lead, so it's clear what the results mean.

diary-study.summary: Participants recording real experiences over a period.
diary-study.description: In a diary study, participants record what happens to them as it happens over days or weeks. Times of day, repetitions, and habits that a single interview misses show up between the entries.

behavioral-heatmap.summary: Comparing where people click and how far they scroll.
behavioral-heatmap.description: A behavioral heatmap overlays in color where many visitors clicked on a page and how far they scrolled. It finds clicks piling up on things that can't be clicked and scrolling that stops before important content.

funnel-analysis.summary: Checking progress through each step and where people drop off.
funnel-analysis.description: Funnel analysis counts how many people remain at each defined step, such as from viewing a product to completing payment. Comparing the rates of moving to the next step shows where most people leave, and splitting by device or source can move that point.
